document.title: Task 2 · Online learning
document.text:
Online courses have become an established part of higher education, raising questions about whether physical classrooms are still necessary. Some people value the flexibility of remote study, while others emphasise direct interaction on campus. In my view, online learning is a useful alternative for some courses, but a blended approach usually offers a stronger university experience.

The main argument for online education is that it allows students to organise study around other responsibilities. Someone who works full time or cares for a family member may find it difficult to attend lectures at fixed hours. Recorded lessons can remove this obstacle and allow difficult explanations to be reviewed. Online courses can also widen access for people who live far from a university. These benefits are substantial, provided that students have a suitable device, a stable connection and access to academic support when they need it.

However, attending university involves more than receiving information. In seminars, students must respond to unfamiliar arguments and explain their ideas to other people. Teachers can notice confusion and adjust a discussion immediately, while students can build relationships through informal conversations before and after class. Practical subjects present an additional difficulty for fully online courses. A nursing student, for example, needs supervised practice with equipment and patients, not merely demonstrations on a screen. Although simulations are useful preparation, they cannot reproduce every aspect of professional work.

I therefore favour a combination of digital and face-to-face teaching. Universities could provide recorded lectures for independent study and reserve classroom time for debate, practical work and individual feedback. This arrangement would retain flexibility without assuming that every educational activity can be transferred online. Ultimately, the method should depend on what students need to learn, rather than on a universal preference for either technology or traditional classrooms.
document.prompt:
WRITING TASK 2
Allow about 40 minutes.

Some people believe that online courses can replace classroom teaching at universities. Others believe that attending classes in person is essential. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Support your answer with reasons and relevant examples. Write at least 250 words.
PPB! original practice material.

annotations.quote: Online courses have become an established part of higher education, raising questions about whether physical classrooms are still necessary.
annotations.label: Position and scope
annotations.body: Names both perspectives and states a blended position. The answer must discuss each view; merely listing benefits of online study would leave the task incomplete.

annotations.quote: The main argument for online education is that it allows students to organise study around other responsibilities.
annotations.label: Developed argument
annotations.body: The working learner example explains why flexible timing improves access. The final condition about devices and support qualifies that benefit rather than assuming equal access.

annotations.quote: However, attending university involves more than receiving information.
annotations.label: Counterpoint and response
annotations.body: Seminar interaction and supervised nursing practice are distinct reasons for face-to-face learning. The nursing example is relevant because it exposes a limit of recorded demonstrations.

annotations.quote: I therefore favour a combination of digital and face-to-face teaching.
annotations.label: Synthesis
annotations.body: Combines recorded lectures with practical classroom time. This is a reasoned synthesis of the two views, not an unexplained preference for technology.
